note:
The household of Frederick Stanley Kipping, professor of chemistry, on Clumber Crescent South on the 1921 return, transcribed by A. Hagues. Ten of the eleven people on the schedule are here, all bound by number; none is created and none carried a 1921 census row before this.

**These rows are deliberately left unfiled.** The crescent holds five houses - 3, 5, 7, 9 and Clumber Court - and five households were returned on it in 1921. Three are settled: Kirkaldy at number 3 by the professor's will, Lewenz at number 7 by the schedule's own house number, and Jardine at number 9 by the family's presence there in 1901, 1911 and 1939. That leaves **5 Clumber Crescent South and Clumber Court** for this household and for the McCraith household, and **nothing decides which is which**. Wright's Directory prints two Perry households on the crescent without numbers in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16 - Mrs John Maddock Perry and John Thorpe Perry - and John Thorpe Perry is returned at number 5 in 1911, so the other Perry household is presumably at Clumber Court; but neither Perry connects to Kipping or to McCraith. Kipping, Kirkaldy, Lewenz and Wigglesworth appear in no volume of the directory at all, so that source is exhausted. Rather than interpolate the enumerator's walk, the rows are created under the address the return gives and left in the unfiled queue. See [[kipping-mccraith-which-house]].

**Florence Holland is missing from this file on purpose.** The schedule has eleven people; the eleventh is Florence Holland, mother-in-law, 78, born in Manchester. The record's Florence Holland (#1329) has the right birth year but her 1921 census row is the one belonging to a **different Florence Holland** - a maid of 39 born in Nottingham, returned at 23 Cavendish Crescent South the same night. The importer binds on an exact unique name, and with only one Florence Holland in the record the maid's row was hung on the mother-in-law. The row itself shows the join: it carries the maid's age of 39 beside the mother-in-law's Manchester birthplace. **Importing her here would either fill blanks on the wrong woman's row or create a duplicate**, so she is held back until the two women are separated by hand, and then wants a file of her own.

**The unfiled page will show this as two households, and it is one.** The splitter starts a new household at every Head and at a second Wife in the same block. Lily Kipping is returned as Wife and Doris May Jinks, wife of the visiting lecturer, is also returned as Wife, so the group will break in two on screen. The relationships are recorded exactly as the enumerator wrote them and have not been adjusted to make the display tidy.

**Two published lives settle his career but not his house.** F. Challenger's Royal Society obituary notice of 1950 and N. R. Thomas's paper of 2010 between them give his birth, parentage, career and death in full, and they are now in his biography. **Neither names his address in The Park**, so neither does anything for the question of which house this household occupied. Challenger does give a different Nottingham address - 40 Magdala Road, where he kept about fifty chickens on the tennis lawn - in a passage about the First World War years, so the relation of that address to this 1921 return is unknown and no property link is made from it. Thomas has him a regular at the Nottingham Park Tennis Club, an institution of the estate that the record does not yet hold at all.

**Three corrections the import cannot make.** First, both sources spell him **Frederic** Stanley Kipping, and the record and the census both have Frederick; an import never renames, so **#1325 wants renaming to Frederic Stanley Kipping**. Second, he was born on **16 August 1863**, where the record holds 1864; an import never overwrites a birth year, and because the years disagree the birth date is refused as well, so both want setting by hand. Third, **Florence Holland (#1329) has the wrong birthplace**: her record gives Nottingham, which belongs to the Holyrood House maid, while this schedule gives Manchester for the mother-in-law. Both published lives of Kipping say the Holland sisters were granddaughters of Charles Allen Duval, so their mother was a Duval who married into the Holland family; but Duval was born at Beaumaris in Anglesey and only settled in Manchester, so that descent does not by itself put a Manchester birth on her. The case for the two women being different rests on the two schedules, which are clear enough without him - see [[holland-sisters-duval-line]]. A birthplace already filled cannot in any event be corrected by an import.

**A college household.** The head is professor of chemistry to the Council of University College, Nottingham; his son Frederick Barry is a chemistry student; and John Clarence Jinks, staying in the house with his wife and small daughter, lectures in pharmaceutics to the same Council. Adam Willis Kirkaldy, professor of economics at that college, was living four doors away at number 3 on the same night. Frederick Stanley Kipping is likely to be a figure of some standing in his subject and is worth checking for the notables page, but nothing about his career is asserted here beyond what the schedule gives.

Ages are as the enumerator wrote them, so a birth year worked back from one may be a year out either way.
source: 1921 census, Clumber Crescent South, the Kipping household, transcribed by A. Hagues. Life of the head from F. Challenger, 'Frederic Stanley Kipping 1863-1949', Obituary Notices of Fellows of the Royal Society, vol. 7 no. 19 (1950), pp. 183-219, and from N. R. Thomas, 'Frederic Stanley Kipping - Pioneer in Silicon Chemistry: His Life and Legacy', Silicon 2 (2010), pp. 187-193, doi 10.1007/s12633-010-9051-x, distributed under a Creative Commons Attribution Noncommercial licence; both supplied by A. Hagues. Supporting: Wright's Directory of Nottingham 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, Clumber Crescent South; the 1911 return for 5 Clumber Crescent South.

people.bio:
Chemist, who named the silicones. He was born at Higher Broughton in Manchester on 16 August 1863, the eldest son of James Stanley Kipping, who held a post in the Manchester branch of the Bank of England, and his wife Julia; his mother's father was the artist Charles Allen Duval (1810-1872), born at Beaumaris in Anglesey and long settled in Manchester as a portrait painter and photographer. From Manchester Grammar School he went to Owens College, took a London B.Sc. in 1882, and spent three years as a chemist to the Manchester Gas Department before going to Munich in 1886 to work under W. H. Perkin junior in von Baeyer's institute. Munich gave him a doctorate summa cum laude, and in 1887 London made him the first candidate ever awarded its D.Sc. on the strength of research alone.

In March 1888 he married his cousin Lily Holland, daughter of W. T. Holland J.P. of Bridgwater and granddaughter of the same C. A. Duval. Perkin married her elder sister and Arthur Lapworth another, so the three chemists whose work shaped British organic chemistry between 1895 and 1930 were brothers-in-law. With Perkin he wrote the textbook known to generations of students simply as 'Perkin and Kipping', first published in 1894 and still being revised at his death.

He was elected to the Royal Society in 1897 at the age of thirty-four, and in the same year took the chair of chemistry at University College, Nottingham, in succession to Professor Frank Clowes, holding it until 1936. He was given the task of planning the chemistry department of the new University College in 1924 and entered it in 1928, and he had been appointed the first Sir Jesse Boot Professor of Chemistry in 1920, on an endowment of twenty thousand pounds from Jesse Boot of Boots the Chemists, later Baron Trent, whose further gift provided the new campus in the western suburbs. During the First World War he and his staff worked on preparing synthetic drugs then unobtainable in Britain, and he lectured in musketry and map-reading to the Officers' Training Corps and ran a miniature rifle range in an old clay-pit.

His life's work was silicon chemistry: fifty-seven papers between 1899 and 1944, among them the series titled 'Organic derivatives of silicon', fifty-one parts running from 1907 to 1944. He coined the word silicone in 1904, and thought the substances themselves sticky messes of no particular use. Within a few years of his death those same silicone polymers had won worldwide recognition as plastics, insulating materials and lubricants, and by 2000 the industry built on them was valued at more than eight billion dollars a year.

On moving to Nottingham he became a regular at the Nottingham Park Tennis Club on the estate itself, and golfed at Hollinwell with the linguist Professor Ernest Weekley on Wednesdays from eleven until three or four. He kept three or four allotments and some fifty chickens on the tennis lawn at 40 Magdala Road, and was remembered by his pupils for a dry humour and an exacting standard of accuracy. He retired from the chair in 1936, was made Emeritus Professor, delivered the Royal Society's Bakerian Lecture on organic derivatives of silicon in the same year, and continued research at Shakespeare Street until 1939, when he moved to Criccieth. He died there on 1 May 1949, aged 85. The Arkwright Building in Shakespeare Street, where his laboratories stood from 1897 to 1928, carries a plaque recording his study of crystalline silicones, and the School of Chemistry at Nottingham was given a Royal Society of Chemistry Historic Chemical Landmark in his honour on 17 March 2004. His son Frederic Barry Kipping, twenty and a chemistry student when this census was taken, became a university lecturer in chemistry at Cambridge and joined the revision of his father's textbook.
